text: A gaming company stores player session data. Traffic is close to zero most of the day but spikes unpredictably during tournaments. The team wants a database with no servers to provision that charges per request. Which option meets these requirements?

options.text: Amazon RDS for MySQL on a larger DB instance class
Amazon DynamoDB in on-demand capacity mode
Amazon DynamoDB in provisioned capacity mode with a fixed capacity
An Amazon Redshift provisioned cluster

explanation: DynamoDB is serverless, and on-demand mode bills per read and write request while scaling automatically with unpredictable traffic. Provisioned mode with fixed capacity charges for the capacity you set whether it is used or not and does not suit unpredictable spikes.

text: A company runs its order database on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. The database must keep running with automatic failover if the Availability Zone that hosts it becomes unavailable. What should the company configure?

options.text: A read replica in the same Availability Zone
A larger DB instance class
An Amazon ElastiCache cluster in front of the database
A Multi-AZ deployment

explanation: A Multi-AZ deployment keeps a synchronous standby in another Availability Zone and fails over to it automatically. A read replica is for read scaling and is not promoted automatically, and a replica in the same AZ would fail with it.

text: A company moves a self-managed MySQL database from Amazon EC2 to Amazon RDS for MySQL. Which tasks will AWS now handle for the company? (Choose two.)

options.text: Patching the operating system of the database host
Designing the database schema and indexes
Tuning slow SQL queries written by the application team
Taking automated backups that allow point-in-time restore
Deciding which users are allowed to connect to the database

explanation: With Amazon RDS, AWS patches the operating system and database software and takes automated backups with point-in-time restore. Schema design, query tuning and control of database access remain the customer's responsibility.

text: Analysts run heavy reporting queries against a production Amazon RDS for MySQL database, and the application becomes slow during these reports. The company wants to offload the reporting reads with minimal changes. What should the company do?

options.text: Enable Multi-AZ and send the reports to the standby
Move the reports to AWS Database Migration Service
Create a read replica and point the reporting queries at it
Increase the backup retention period

explanation: A read replica is a read-only copy that takes read traffic, such as reports, away from the primary DB instance. The standby in a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment cannot serve read traffic; it exists only for failover.

text: A retail company wants to run complex SQL analytics over several years of sales data collected from many sources to produce business intelligence reports. Which AWS service is designed for this workload?

options.text: Amazon Redshift
Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon ElastiCache
Amazon DocumentDB

explanation: Amazon Redshift is a managed data warehouse built for analytical (OLAP) SQL queries over large data sets. DynamoDB is an operational NoSQL database for fast key-based access, not for large analytical queries.

text: A company plans to move an on-premises Oracle database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. Before the data is moved, the tables, views and stored procedures must be converted to the new engine. Which AWS tool converts the schema?

options.text: AWS DataSync
AWS Backup
Amazon RDS read replicas
AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT)

explanation: AWS SCT (or DMS Schema Conversion) converts database schemas and code objects from one engine to another for heterogeneous migrations. AWS DataSync moves files and objects between storage systems; it does not convert database schemas.

text: Which statements about Amazon DynamoDB are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Customers must choose a weekly maintenance window for engine patching
On-demand capacity mode charges per request and needs no capacity planning
It supports SQL joins across tables like a relational database
Each table is limited to a single Availability Zone
Global tables replicate a table across multiple AWS Regions

explanation: On-demand mode bills per read and write request and scales without capacity planning, and global tables replicate data across the Regions you choose. DynamoDB has no maintenance windows, does not support joins, and replicates data across three Availability Zones by default.

text: A social media start-up needs to store members and their connections so it can quickly answer questions such as "Which friends of my friends like the same bands?" Which AWS database service fits this data best?

options.text: Amazon Timestream
Amazon Neptune
Amazon Redshift
Amazon ElastiCache

explanation: Amazon Neptune is a graph database built to store and query highly connected data and relationships. Timestream is for time series data such as sensor readings, not for relationships between people.

text: An application on Amazon RDS reads the same product details thousands of times per minute, and the database is under heavy read load. The company wants to keep frequently read data in memory to reduce latency and database load. Which service should it add?

options.text: Amazon Redshift
AWS Database Migration Service
Amazon ElastiCache
Amazon DocumentDB

explanation: Amazon ElastiCache is a managed in-memory cache (Valkey, Redis OSS or Memcached) that serves frequently read data quickly and offloads the database. Redshift is a data warehouse for analytics and does not act as a cache in front of RDS.

text: Which are characteristics of Amazon Aurora? (Choose two.)

options.text: It is a NoSQL key-value database with no schema
It runs only on customer-managed Amazon EC2 instances
It is compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL
It is designed as a graph database for connected data
Its storage keeps copies of the data across three Availability Zones

explanation: Aurora is a managed relational engine compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL, and its cluster volume stores copies of the data across three Availability Zones. It is not a NoSQL or graph database, and AWS manages it through Amazon RDS rather than on your own EC2 instances.
